items.title: Social Facilitation vs. Social Loafing
items.content: **Different group effects:** Social facilitation describes performance changes in another person's presence, often improvement on well-learned or simple tasks and impairment on difficult or novel tasks under particular evaluation conditions. Social loafing describes reduced individual effort when contributions are pooled and difficult to identify. Task complexity, identifiability, group meaning, skill, evaluation, coordination, and culture moderate both; neither is an inevitable "people work better or worse in groups" rule.

items.title: Groupthink
items.content: **Groupthink as contingent decision model:** Janis proposed that cohesion combined with structural faults and provocative context can foster concurrence seeking, self-censorship, pressure on dissent, illusions of unanimity, and poor information search. Cohesion alone neither causes defective decisions nor proves groupthink after a bad outcome. Examine decision procedures, alternatives, expertise, dissent, leadership, records, incentives, and outcome-independent evidence; safeguards include impartial leadership, independent subgroups, outside critique, and second-chance review.

items.title: Persuasion: ELM & Foot-in-Door
items.content: **Two distinct persuasion cues:** Under high motivation and ability, ELM predicts greater scrutiny of issue-relevant arguments; careful thought can yield acceptance, rejection, or no change. Under lower elaboration, source and contextual cues may exert greater influence, but variables can play multiple roles. Foot-in-the-door research finds that agreeing to a small request can sometimes increase later compliance; it does not guarantee agreement, and similarity, timing, identity, pressure, and context moderate the effect.

items.title: Self-Serving Bias & Just World
items.content: **Attribution cautions:** Self-serving bias describes a tendency in some contexts to claim more personal credit for favorable than unfavorable outcomes. Just-world belief concerns assumptions that outcomes are deserved, which can support victim blame when situational constraints are ignored. Neither pattern is universal or diagnosed from one explanation. Accuracy, culture, power, controllability, self-protection, information, and actor-observer perspective must be assessed separately.

items.title: Leadership Theories
items.content: **Leadership frameworks:** Trait and behavioral approaches ask who leads and what leaders do; contingency models examine fit among style, task, followers, and situation; transactional leadership emphasizes exchanges; transformational leadership emphasizes vision, meaning, and development. These are overlapping research lenses, not fixed leader types or guarantees of effectiveness. Outcome criterion, ethics, power, culture, team composition, implementation, and measurement determine what conclusions are defensible.

items.title: Job Satisfaction & Motivation Theories
items.content: **Work-attitude and motivation map:** Job satisfaction is an evaluative attitude with modest, variable associations with performance, withdrawal, and well-being. Expectancy, equity, goal-setting, reinforcement, job-characteristics, and self-determination theories address different mechanisms and levels. No theory predicts every worker, and satisfaction does not by itself cause performance. Define the outcome and job context, examine resources and constraints, and use validated measures before selecting an intervention.

items.title: Types of Conformity
items.content: **Conformity distinctions:** Public compliance can occur without private acceptance; identification involves responding in relation to a valued group or role; internalization reflects greater private acceptance. Normative and informational influence are proposed processes, not motives directly observed from behavior. Response visibility, ambiguity, unanimity, expertise, group identity, culture, stakes, and dissent affect yielding, and one answer cannot reveal a permanent conformity type.

items.title: Attitude Formation & Change
items.content: **Attitude-change cue:** Attitudes can involve affective, cognitive, and behavioral information, but those components need not agree. Persuasion depends on message, source, recipient, channel, prior attitude, motivation, ability, and context. High elaboration increases sensitivity to argument quality rather than guaranteeing acceptance or permanence. Behavior can sometimes influence attitudes through dissonance or self-perception processes, but observed change does not uniquely identify one mechanism.

items.title: Minority Influence
items.content: **Minority-influence cue:** A consistent minority can prompt attention and private reconsideration, especially when it appears autonomous and flexible rather than rigid. Consistency is neither sufficient nor universally persuasive; credibility, timing, group identity, conflict, social cost, task, and majority response matter. Public compliance and private conversion require different evidence, and disagreement by itself does not show that the minority caused lasting attitude change.

items.title: Prosocial Behavior & Altruism
items.content: **Helping-behavior cue:** Presence of others is associated on average with lower individual intervention in many studies, but danger, competence, communication, relationships, and supportive bystanders can attenuate or reverse the pattern. Diffusion, ambiguity, audience inhibition, empathy, norms, and cost-reward appraisals are possible mechanisms, not traits inferred from nonhelping. In emergencies, social explanation must never delay scene safety, emergency contact, and action within training.

items.title: Motivation Theories - I/O
items.content: **I/O motivation map:** Expectancy theory links effort, performance expectancy, instrumentality, and valued outcomes; equity theory concerns perceived input-outcome fairness; goal-setting emphasizes specific challenging accepted goals with feedback; reinforcement focuses on consequences; self-determination distinguishes autonomous and controlled motivation. These are conditional models, not formulas that guarantee effort. Ability, resources, role clarity, justice, culture, safety, and goal conflict require separate assessment.

items.title: Job Analysis Methods
items.content: **Job-analysis cue:** Interviews, observation, questionnaires, work diaries, critical incidents, and existing records provide different evidence about tasks and worker requirements. Task-oriented and worker-oriented analyses answer related but distinct questions. No single method is automatically best; combine knowledgeable sources and methods appropriate to the job, document sampling and change, address accessibility and bias, and connect specifications to the intended selection or performance criterion.

items.title: Insanity Defense Standards
items.content: **Legal responsibility, not diagnosis:** M'Naghten, irresistible-impulse, Model Penal Code, and product-test formulations are historical legal standards. Current tests, burdens, admissibility, verdict options, and terminology vary by jurisdiction and can change. Competence to proceed and criminal responsibility at the time of the act are separate questions. Mental disorder alone does not establish insanity, and memorized state counts, prevalence claims, or "broadest" rankings cannot replace current controlling law.

items.title: Performance Appraisal Rater Errors
items.content: **Rater-error recognition:** Halo or horns, leniency or severity, central tendency, recency, contrast, and similarity are hypotheses about how a rater may distort job-performance judgments. Diagnose the pattern from repeated, job-relevant evidence rather than disagreement alone. Behaviorally anchored criteria, representative observation periods, contemporaneous documentation, frame-of-reference training, and appropriately selected multiple raters can reduce some vulnerabilities; no safeguard makes ratings bias-free.
